cards.back: **Primary productivity** is the rate at which producers make organic molecules from inorganic substances using light energy, given per unit area.
cards.hint: Think about who starts the food for every other organism, and how fast it happens.

cards.front: Which symbol equation links net primary productivity to gross primary productivity and respiratory loss?
cards.back: $\mathrm{NPP}=\mathrm{GPP}-R$, where $R$ is the respiratory loss, in units such as $\mathrm{kJ\,m^{-2}\,year^{-1}}$. NPP is the energy left in new plant material after respiration.
cards.hint: Start from the energy fixed in photosynthesis, then consider what the plant spends.

cards.front: Why can improving one condition fail to raise productivity?
cards.back: A **limiting factor** is the variable in shortest supply. It sets the rate even when other conditions are favourable, so improving anything else makes no difference until it is raised.
cards.hint: Think about a chain that is only as strong as its weakest link.

cards.front: A woodland has a GPP of $12\,000\,\mathrm{kJ\,m^{-2}\,year^{-1}}$ and respiratory loss of $5400\,\mathrm{kJ\,m^{-2}\,year^{-1}}$. What is its NPP?
Why is dry mass, rather than fresh mass, used to estimate biomass?
cards.back: Plants contain varying amounts of water. **Dry mass**, the mass after drying to a constant value, removes this variation and gives a fairer measure of organic material.
cards.hint: Consider how much water two plants of the same species might hold.

cards.front: What are the steps for finding the energy content of dry plant material?
cards.back: 1) Burn a known dry mass in a **calorimeter**. 2) Measure the temperature rise of a known mass of water. 3) Calculate the energy released. 4) Divide by the dry mass to get energy per gram.
cards.hint: Start with what happens to the sample inside the apparatus.

cards.front: Burning 2.50 g of dry plant material releases 42.5 kJ of heat. What is the energy released per gram?

cards.back: The **total** chemical energy fixed by producers in photosynthesis, per unit area per unit time.
cards.hint: Compare it with what is left after the producers respire.

cards.front: Why is net primary productivity the energy available to consumers?
cards.back: NPP is the energy stored in new plant tissue after respiratory loss, so organisms that feed on plants can take it in.
cards.hint: Think about what is actually built into plant material.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say that higher temperature always raises productivity?
cards.back: Above the best temperature, **enzymes are denatured** and productivity falls. Warmth only raises productivity up to that optimum.
cards.hint: Think about what happens to enzymes when they get too hot.

cards.front: How does a water shortage reduce primary productivity?
cards.back: Leaf **pores close**, so less carbon dioxide enters the leaf. Less carbon is fixed in photosynthesis, so productivity falls.
cards.hint: Trace the path from the soil, through the leaf, to carbon dioxide uptake.

cards.front: Which mineral ion does a producer need to make amino acids?
cards.back: **Nitrate**, which supplies the nitrogen needed to build amino acids.
cards.hint: Think about which element all amino acids contain.

cards.front: Why is productivity high in tropical rainforests but low in polar regions?
cards.back: Rainforests have warmth, plentiful water and strong light for much of the year. Polar regions are cold and have a short growing season.
cards.hint: Compare the temperature, water and season length of the two places.

cards.front: Why does productivity in a temperate habitat usually peak in spring and summer?
cards.back: Days are long and leaves are present, so plants can capture more light for photosynthesis.
cards.hint: Compare winter with summer for light and plant cover.
